data.html:
Lesson Overview

In our last lesson, you organized your teams and planned production schedules using organizational charts and Gantt charts — learning to manage people and processes the way a skilled engineer manages a real project. Today, we're moving into a phase that engineers often overlook until it's too late: Death & Recycling.

What happens to your mousetrap car once it's finished its race? What happens to the materials — the wood, the wire, the rubber bands — after the project is done? Engineering isn't just about building something that works. It's about planning for the entire lifecycle of a product, from the first sketch all the way to the moment it's no longer useful. In this lesson, you'll explore how thoughtful engineers design with the end in mind, and how that mindset connects directly to our responsibility as stewards of God's creation.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Define the Death & Recycling phase within the Creationeering™ framework.
  • Identify different end-of-life options for engineered products — reuse, recycling, and disposal.
  • Explain how material selection impacts the recyclability and sustainability of a product.
  • Apply end-of-life thinking to the design and construction of your mousetrap car.
  • Reflect on your role as a steward of God's creation through responsible engineering choices.

items.definition: The final phase of a product's lifecycle — addressing what happens to materials once the product's useful life is over, including converting them into new materials or products.
A method engineers use to evaluate the environmental impact of a product across its entire life, from raw material extraction all the way to disposal.
Designing and operating systems so that resources are used responsibly, without preventing future generations from meeting their own needs.
The process of converting used materials into new materials and objects instead of sending them to a landfill.
Using a product or material again for the same or a different purpose without significantly changing it.
The act of getting rid of waste, typically through landfills or incineration — generally the least sustainable end-of-life option.
The specific characteristics of a material — such as strength, durability, and recyclability — that determine how suitable it is for a given application.
The responsible care and protection of something worth preserving — especially God's creation.

data.html:
God's Built-In Renewal Cycles

Before there were engineers, there was the ultimate Designer. God didn't just create a universe that works — He created one that renews itself. Think about the seasons: spring, summer, autumn, winter, and then spring again. Or the water cycle, where water evaporates from the ocean, forms clouds, rains down on the mountains, and flows back to the sea. Nothing is wasted. Everything returns.

Ecclesiastes 1:4–7 captures this beautifully:

"Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises and the sun sets, and hurries back to where it rises. The wind blows to the south and turns to the north; round and round it goes, ever returning on its course. All streams flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full; to the place the streams come from, there they return again."

— Ecclesiastes 1:4–7

This passage is more than poetry — it's an engineering principle. While individual things have a beginning and an end, God designed the larger system so that nothing is truly lost. Materials transform. Energy moves. Cycles renew. As engineers, we're called to imitate that wisdom by designing products with their entire lifecycle in mind, not just the moment they work best.

What Is End-of-Life Planning?

Every product eventually reaches the end of its useful life. A mousetrap car stops rolling. A phone becomes outdated. A bridge gets replaced. The question engineers ask is: then what?

End-of-life planning is the practice of deciding — before you even finish building — what will happen to your product and its materials when it's no longer needed. There are three main paths a product can take:

  • Reuse — Parts are used again, either for the same purpose or a new one. Your mousetrap car's wheels might become part of a cart. The wood frame might become a shelf. Reuse is the most resource-efficient option because it skips the energy cost of breaking things down.
  • Recycling — Materials are broken down and converted into new raw materials. Metal axles can be melted and reformed. Some plastics can be shredded and re-molded. Recycling requires energy, but it keeps materials out of landfills.
  • Disposal — Materials go to a landfill or are incinerated. This is the last resort. It wastes materials and can harm the environment. Good engineering tries to minimize how much ends up here.

data.caption: A diagram showing three end-of-life pathways for a simple product — arrows branching from a used item toward three labeled boxes: Reuse, Recycle, and Dispose — with a circular arrow connecting Reuse and Recycle back to 'New Product'

data.html:
How Material Choice Shapes End-of-Life

Here's something most people don't think about when they grab a piece of balsa wood or a rubber band at the supply table: the material you choose determines what happens to your project when it's over.

Engineers call this thinking about material properties. A material's properties aren't just about how strong or light it is — they also include whether it can be recycled, how long it takes to break down naturally, and whether it releases harmful chemicals when it's discarded.

Consider some of the materials in your mousetrap car:

  • Wood — Natural, biodegradable, and often reusable. A great choice from a lifecycle perspective.
  • Metal (wire, axles, springs) — Highly recyclable. Metal can be melted down and reused almost indefinitely without losing quality.
  • Rubber bands — Natural rubber is biodegradable, but synthetic rubber is harder to recycle and breaks down slowly.
  • Plastic components — Recyclability depends heavily on the type of plastic. Some plastics are widely recycled; others are not accepted by most facilities.
  • Glue and adhesives — These can contaminate other materials and make them harder to recycle. Mechanical fasteners (screws, clips) are often a more sustainable choice.

When you design with the end in mind, you start asking questions like: Can this part be removed easily? Can these two materials be separated for recycling? Is there a biodegradable alternative? That's lifecycle thinking.

Lifecycle Assessment: Seeing the Whole Picture

A lifecycle assessment (LCA) is a tool engineers use to evaluate the environmental impact of a product at every stage — not just when it's being used, but when raw materials are extracted, when it's manufactured, when it's shipped, and when it's eventually discarded or recycled.

Think of it like drawing a timeline for your mousetrap car. Stage 1 is the raw materials — trees cut for wood, mines dug for metal. Stage 2 is manufacturing — cutting, shaping, assembling. Stage 3 is use — the car races down the track. Stage 4 is end-of-life — the car is taken apart, parts reused, materials recycled or disposed.

A good engineer looks at that whole timeline and asks: where can we reduce harm? Where can we close the loop so materials cycle back rather than pile up?

data.caption: A circular lifecycle diagram for a simple wooden mousetrap car showing four labeled stages connected by arrows: Raw Materials → Manufacturing → Use → End-of-Life (Reuse/Recycle/Dispose), with a dotted feedback arrow from End-of-Life back to Raw Materials

data.html:
Applying End-of-Life Thinking to Your Mousetrap Car

Now it's time to think about your own build. Your mousetrap car isn't just a race vehicle — it's a real engineering project, and that means it deserves real end-of-life planning.

As you look at your car, consider these questions:

  • Which parts can be reused as-is — maybe in a future project or donated to next year's class?
  • Which materials can be recycled — separated from other materials and sent to the appropriate stream?
  • What parts will likely end up in the trash, and could a design change have prevented that?
  • Were there material choices you made — like using a lot of hot glue — that make it harder to take the car apart at the end?

This kind of reflection is what separates a good engineer from a great one. Building something that works is the starting point. Building something that works and can be responsibly retired — that's mastery.

Design for Disassembly: One of the best sustainability strategies engineers use is called Design for Disassembly — building products so they can be easily taken apart into separate materials at the end of their life. When you review your mousetrap car, ask yourself: could someone take this apart in under two minutes and sort the materials into wood, metal, and rubber? If not, think about what you'd change in your next design.

Stewardship in Action

The word stewardship means caring responsibly for something that belongs to someone else. For engineers, stewardship means recognizing that the materials we use — wood, metal, rubber, plastic — come from a creation that belongs to God. We are borrowing them, in a sense. And how we return them matters.

Ecclesiastes reminds us that streams return to the sea. Water doesn't disappear — it cycles. God built renewal into His creation. When engineers design for recycling and reuse, they're not just following environmental guidelines. They're participating in that same cycle of renewal that God wove into the fabric of the universe.

Your mousetrap car is a small project. But the habits you build here — thinking about lifecycle, choosing materials wisely, planning for end-of-life — are the same habits that professional engineers use when designing bridges, phones, cars, and buildings. Start small, think big.

Common Mistake: Many students think end-of-life planning is something you do after the project is finished. In reality, it needs to happen before and during the build. Material choices made in Week 1 determine what's recyclable in Week 8. Once glue is applied or parts are permanently fused, those decisions can't easily be undone. Plan ahead.

data.title: Going Deeper: What Is a Circular Economy?
data.html:
In traditional manufacturing, products follow a straight line: make it, use it, throw it away. Engineers and economists call this a linear economy. The problem is obvious — it eventually runs out of materials and fills up landfills.

A circular economy is a different model, inspired by natural systems like the ones God built into creation. In a circular economy, materials are kept in use for as long as possible. Products are designed to be repaired, reused, remanufactured, and recycled — with as little waste as possible.

Companies like Patagonia (clothing), Interface (carpet tiles), and Apple (electronics) have started building circular economy principles into their products. Patagonia repairs worn jackets. Interface tiles can be individually replaced and recycled. Apple designs iPhones to be disassembled by robots and sorts recovered metals back into the manufacturing supply chain.

As a future engineer, you might work on products that operate within a circular economy. The foundation you're building right now — thinking about lifecycle, material choice, and end-of-life — is exactly the mindset that makes circular design possible.
